details:
Title: GravityGap

Turning NASA’s microgravity fire experiments into fire-safety guidance for crewed missions, and showing exactly where the data stops.

Description:

GravityGap is an interactive dashboard that turns NASA’s microgravity combustion research into fire-safety guidance for crewed missions.

We hand-curated 13 low-gravity combustion investigations across flammability (BASS, Saffire), fire detection (SAME, DAFT), suppression (FLEX), and flames and droplets (CFI, ACME).

Users can rank the investigations by relevance to crew environments, compare them side by side, and ask questions to an AI assistant that answers only from the curated records

Problem:

Future crews on the Moon may live in atmospheres very different from Earth’s. The challenge statement describes Moon habitats at 30% oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less, against 21% oxygen and 14.7 psi on Earth. Higher oxygen makes materials much more flammable.

The research that could inform those designs is hard to use:

  • The data is heterogeneous: text and numbers, plus large image and video sets.
  • The schema differs between investigations, so oxygen %, airflow and sensors sit in different places or are missing.
  • Relevance to future habitats is stated nowhere.
  • Nobody can compare investigations quickly.

Solution:

GravityGap has four parts, all live in the deployed app.

  • Explorer. A table and cards for the 13 investigations. Each shows its objective, fuels, oxygen range, pressure range, airflow, variables varied and sensors. Every field carries a status of verified, unverified or not_available, and a detail page lists the sources behind each value. A permanent banner states on every page that no partial-gravity data exists.
  • Relevance ranking. Two sliders weight the ISS and a Moon base. Each investigation’s score is shown with a per-row breakdown
  • Compare view. Two to four investigations side by side, with the fields that differ marked.
  • Grounded AI Q&A. Gemini is called from the server only. It answers from the curated records, and the server checks every claim and number against the stored values. Every claim links to its source record. If PSI holds no data, as with partial gravity, the app says so instead of guessing. Off-topic requests are refused.

How we used space agency data:

  • NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS): technical reports and papers describing the experiments. We curated each record’s test conditions (fuels, oxygen range, pressure range, airflow, sensors, variables varied) by hand from these reports, and each value carries a source title and URL.
  • NASA Science mission pages: experiment and mission pages for the same investigations. We used them alongside NTRS to curate and cross-check each record, and they are listed as sources on the detail pages.
  • Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI): we used it only to find the experiments. The curated data comes from NTRS and NASA Science pages.

Tech stack:

  • Front end: Next.js (App Router), TypeScript in strict mode, Tailwind CSS
  • Data and validation: curated JSON validated at build time with Zod 4
  • AI: Gemini, model “Gemini Hydrogen”, via the @google/genai SDK, server-side only
  • Rate limiting: Upstash Redis
  • Deployment: Vercel and Google Cloud

How we built it:

We are Future_Fusions, and we built GravityGap during the 48-hour NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Mumbai. Three problems shaped the journey.

  1. Choosing a challenge. The event offered 14 challenges. Picking one was our first decision, and we chose Flame in Freefall.
  2. Designing the architecture. We settled on a static-first design. The data is bundled at build time and validated by one schema. Filtering, scoring and comparison run in the browser, and only the AI route needs a server, so a failure of the AI service leaves the rest of the app working.
  3. Deployment. Deploying the application on Google Cloud and on Vercel gave us problems, and we worked through them until the app went live.

Future scope:

  • Retrieval step: replace full-set prompting once the dataset passes 60 records, so the AI layer scales.
  • Per-experiment ACME records: split ACME’s six experiments into separate records for finer detail.
  • Rover and Mars profiles: enable these environments once sourced reference values exist.
  • Partial-gravity data: add records, with cited sources, if any source ever publishes them, and remove the gap labels only then.
